newsitem.title: usa: Ethics panel takes up proposed Gingrich punishment.
newsitem.headline: Ethics panel takes up proposed Gingrich punishment.

text.p: A congressional committee met on Friday to consider recommendations on punishment for ethics breaches by House Speaker Newt Gingrich, reported to include a reprimand, a hefty fine and a call for a full federal investigation.

Members of the House of Representatives ethics committee declined comment as they entered the hearing room for a closed morning session, at which they were to receive the final -- and reportedly highly critical -- report on the Gingrich case by special counsel James Cole.
It was expected the committee, bitterly divided down partisan lines, would move into open session to continue its debate of what punishments to recommend to the full House.
A decisive vote by the whole chamber was scheduled for next Tuesday.

Cole's report was not immediately made public but the New York Times and the Baltimore Sun said in Friday's editions that Cole was recommending not only the expected reprimand but a stiff fine. The Sun said that could be more than $100,000.
No incumbent U.S. House speaker has ever been even reprimanded, although that penalty alone would not force Gingrich, a conservative Georgia Republican, to quit the post.

Cole was also said to favour reference of the case to the U.S. Justice Department for full federal investigation, a move that would have the effect of drawing out the Gingrich controversy indefinitely.
Gingrich said in response to reporters' questions on Thursday that "we're going to do whatever we're asked to do and we're going to try to be helpful."

Gingrich, the first Republican re-elected as speaker in 68 years, admitted "with great sadness" on Dec. 21 that he had provided to investigators "in my name and over my signature, inaccurate, incomplete and unreliable statements." He said he had not intended to mislead the committee.

He also acknowledged he had failed to seek legal advice on whether his use of tax-exempt charitable funds for a college course he taught would violate tax laws. The subcommittee did not take a position on whether the law had been broken.
The ethics committee has been battered by controversy.

First its Republican Chairwoman Nancy Johnson of Connecticut cancelled a week of public hearings. Then the committee's top Democrat, Jim McDermott of Washington state, was forced to step aside following disclosure that he had received a tape of an illegally monitored telephone conversation between Gingrich and top aides that was later leaked to the press.

Partisan quarreling over the two developments soured the opening of a new Congress which was supposed to have set a tone of cooperation and bipartisanship at the start of President Bill Clinton's second term.
